Leave-one-region-out cross-validation highlighted limited geographic transferability, particularly for HYB2 and MR4B in the West Sea. Applying the algorithm to Geostationary Ocean Color Imager-II (GOCI-II) imagery revealed algorithm-dependent retrieval magnitudes and spatial patterns; accuracy assessment requires concurrent field observations. These findings identify HYB2 and MR4B as promising candidates for regional refinement and provide a foundation for advancing GOCI-II-based monitoring of coastal aDOM(440).

title: EBSFFormer: An Expert-Behavior-Guided Spatial–Frequency Collaborative Transformer for Remote Sensing Image Super-Resolution
summary: Remote sensing image super-resolution requires local detail and wider structural context. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) designs compared here select or combine expert outputs without explicitly passing behavior statistics to subsequent spatial–frequency restoration. We propose EBSFFormer, which aggregates routing preferences and response-weighted proportions within restoration groups and converts them into channel gains for later spatial and frequency branches. Heterogeneous experts and a content–cumulative-change router supply these statistics. We train on AID and evaluate on AID, DIOR, DOTA, and NWPU-RESISC45 under bicubic ×4 degradation. Across three AID training seeds, EBSFFormer obtains 31.2639 ± 0.0009 dB peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), with mean improvements of 0.0121 dB over MambaIRv2 and 0.1037 dB over SwinIR. Single-checkpoint evaluation on NWPU without fine-tuning gives the highest Y-channel PSNR and structural similarity index (SSIM) among the compared methods and the third-lowest learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). Component ablations, red–green–blue (RGB) metrics, and ground-truth-referenced visual comparisons characterize the reconstruction gains. EBSFFormer has fewer parameters and lower mean latency than MambaIRv2, but the highest peak allocated memory in the runtime comparison.

title: Hyperspectral remote sensing of cover crop traits for decision support in precision nitrogen management
summary: Spaceborne hyperspectral sensors offer opportunities to quantify crop traits and inform variable rate nitrogen management, yet their operational use remains limited. We evaluated PRISMA and EMIT imagery across four winter cover crop seasons in Maryland, U.S., to predict traits required by the open source Cover Crop Nitrogen Calculator (CC-NCALC) decision support tool. Traits included aboveground biomass, nitrogen concentration (N%), non-structural carbohydrates (NSC%), holocellulose (HCL%), and lignin (LIG%). Using these traits as inputs, the CC-NCALC estimates nitrogen credits from cover crops based on decomposition dynamics informed by trait data, soil, and weather conditions. Nitrogen credits are the estimated amount of plant available nitrogen that a cover crop contributes to the subsequently planted cash crop. Trait models were developed using partial least squares regression with several cross validation strategies. Biomass ( R 2 = 0.70–0.87; RMSE = 661–951 kg ha −1 ), NSC% ( R 2 = 0.69–0.72; RMSE = 4.53–7.63%), and HCL% ( R 2 = 0.65–0.70; RMSE = 5.04–7.50%) predictions were strong. But HCL% and NSC% predictions degraded under cross-scene and cross-species validation ( R 2 = 0.47–0.54; RMSE = 6.06–9.18%). N% ( R 2 = 0.15–0.79; RMSE = 0.46–0.74%) and LIG% ( R 2 = 0.02–0.35; RMSE = 1.22–1.83%) predictions were more variable; predictions using EMIT were more accurate than predictions using PRISMA, but both approaches demonstrated the need for further increases in accuracies of retrieval approaches for these two traits. Spring trait maps from April 2024 were ingested into the CC-NCALC to estimate nitrogen credits, which ranged from −14.58 to 45.65 kg N ha −1 , with higher values associated with greater legume biomass. Inter-scene comparisons demonstrate EMIT's increased spectral fidelity and trait prediction accuracy compared to PRISMA. Results demonstrate that integrating spaceborne hyperspectral imagery with decision support systems can generate site-specific nitrogen credit maps, advancing hyperspectral remote sensing toward operational nutrient management. Future missions will be critical to help scale these approaches for routine on-farm use.

title: Spatiotemporal variability in seasonal and interannual InSAR-derived excess ground ice content retrievals using Sentinel-1
summary: The melting of excess ground ice in ice-rich permafrost regions causes elevated ground subsidence through soil thaw consolidation at landscape scales. The increased subsidence due to melting of excess ice is unaccounted for in current InSAR-based retrievals of season thaw depth, or active layer thickness (ALT); this omission may lead to overapproximated ALT estimates compared to in situ. We processed Sentinel-1 interferometric data spanning 2018–2023 over the Drew Point and Teshekpuk Lake region. Using a novel degree-day of thaw regression on InSAR displacement time series, we estimated total seasonal subsidence and found elevated subsidence during warmer years which we attribute to the melting of excess ice. Integrating these seasonal subsidence estimates into the remotely sensed active layer thickness (ReSALT) algorithm yielded consistently overapproximated ALT estimates. In conjunction with independent estimates of ALT, we exploited this positive bias in ReSALT to estimate excess ice within the active layer. We found agreement between InSAR estimates of excess ice and in situ measurements within uncertainty for warmer years. We observed a positive spatial correlation between seasonal subsidence and excess ice in the active layer with proximity to surface hydrological features. Furthermore, we observed that InSAR-derived subsidence decreases with older drained lakes, and InSAR-derived excess ice decreases with increasingly degraded ice wedge polygon type. We discovered that thaw season intensity has a first order effect on the temporal variability of seasonal subsidence and excess ice content, and the success of our method is contingent upon warm thaw seasons.

title: High resolution sediment-specific surface soil moisture retrieval using Sentinel-1 time series and auxiliary data
summary: In this study, we examine the potential of continuous ground moisture monitoring over a mining site using a combination of in-situ soil moisture sensors and multi-sensor SAR images. We focus on assessing and improving methodologies for retrieval of surface soil moisture, i.e. ground moisture, from SAR measurements focusing on detailed in situ reference observations for several key geomaterials, i.e. sediments, typical in the study site. The mining site represents a limestone quarry located in the southeastern Finland. Our hypothesis is that sediment-specific well-calibrated models can be instrumental in improving soil moisture retrieval under different weather conditions to produce spatially explicit soil moisture estimates at high resolution compared to baseline approaches. Studied SAR data are represented by Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band images, while auxiliary datasets include optical Sentinel-2 data. Reference data were collected using IoT enabled capacitance sensors. The reference data were calibrated based on laboratory analyses conducted on the different sediment types studied, including organic soil, clay, gravel, and flotation sand. The examined machine learning (ML) methods include XGBoost, LightGBM, random forest, support vector regression, linear regression and k-nearest neighbors. The performance of ML algorithms was evaluated using different cross-validation techniques including a five-fold approach as well as Leave-One-Sensor-Out (LOSO) to assess predictive accuracy and transferability to unseen sensors. The best performance under random five-fold cross-validation was achieved with the most comprehensive feature set which combines Sentinel-1 backscatter, time-series based soil moisture indices (SMI), Sentinel-2 optical, topographic, and temperature predictors. SHAP analysis revealed that SAR based features such as VH backscatter, traditional SMI derived from VV backscatter, and incidence angle were among the most important multi-source predictors. Adding sediment information improved Sentinel-1-only retrievals by more than 2 vol-%, but provided little additional benefit when richer multi-source feature sets were used. In the best sediment-area-level configurations, RMSE decreased to 0.037–0.050 m 3 m − 3 (3.7-5.0 vol. % points ), with R 2 values reaching 0.90. Accuracy varied by sediment texture, with the lowest errors for clay and organic soil and higher errors for flotation sand and gravel. However, LOSO validation demonstrated substantially weaker and site-dependent transferability: R 2 ranged from 0.45 to 0.67 for organic soil at a southern site and from 0.07 to 0.21 for organic soil at a northern site. Thus, high within-dataset predictive accuracy did not translate uniformly to unseen sensor locations, highlighting the need for broader spatially independent validation.

title: A novel approach for soil moisture retrieval via fusing multi-spaceborne GNSS-R observations in entire Tibetan Plateau
summary: Spaceborne GNSS-Reflectometry (GNSS-R) is a powerful technology for soil moisture (SM) retrieval. However, complex topography and steep slopes over the Tibetan Plateau lead to significant signal loss and sampling sparsity. This study proposes a novel Dirichlet-prior-guided Vision Transformer (DG-ViT) framework to fuse multi-source observations from CYGNSS, Tianmu-1, and the FY-3E/F/G constellation. The novel DG-ViT framework incorporates land cover informed prior guidance into multi-spaceborne surface reflectivity (SR) fusion, and its performance is evaluated against single-source retrievals and traditional machine learning algorithms. To assess generalization, the fused SR was coupled with six mainstream machine learning algorithms (RF, XGBoost, ANN, BP, SVM, and GBDT) for 9 km daily SM retrieval, with multi-scale validation conducted against ERA5 SM and nine in-situ stations. Results demonstrate that the DG-ViT framework achieves a daily SR coverage of 89.49 %, representing an improvement of 20.13 % and 14.32 % over standalone CYGNSS and Tianmu-1 data, respectively. In addition, this fusion strategy overcomes the coverage gap of CYGNSS north of 38°N and compensates for the inability of individual FY-3 missions to support daily SM retrieval. In comparative assessments, the DG-ViT combined with RF yields superior performance (R = 0.955, RMSE = 0.039 cm 3 /cm 3 , bias = 0.000 cm 3 /cm 3 ), markedly enhancing retrieval accuracy relative to results derived from single-source CYGNSS or Tianmu-1 SR. In-situ validation shows ubRMSE values between 0.0232 and 0.0619 cm 3 /cm 3 , a 15.1 % precision gain over ERA5 SM. The proposed DG-ViT combined with RF approach effectively exploits the complementarity among multi-spaceborne GNSS-R observations over the entire Tibetan Plateau, thereby compensating for the signal deficiencies of individual missions. This fusion approach provides a novel perspective for SM retrieval in high-altitude areas, specifically improving daily SR coverage and SM retrieval accuracy through fusion of multi-spaceborne GNSS-R observations with land cover informed prior guidance.

title: Process-informed deep learning for interpretable forested wetland mapping under dense canopy
summary: Canopy-obscured hydrologic signals and gradual wetland–upland transitions hinder the delineation of forested wetlands, particularly when heterogeneous Earth-observation evidence is fused as an unstructured feature stack. We developed a process-informed multi-stream convolutional neural network (CNN) for mapping forested wetlands on a 10-m modelling grid in the Changbai Mountains, China. The model used 85 covariates derived from Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, ALOS-2 PALSAR-2, and Copernicus DEM GLO-30. These covariates were assigned a priori to five predictor streams and processed by separate CNN branches before fusion. Relative to a capacity-matched single-stream baseline, the grouped architecture increased forested-wetland F1 by 3.42 percentage points across five validation folds, whereas the gain on the fixed held-out test set was smaller (+1.03 percentage points). For map production, the probability-averaged five-fold ensemble achieved an overall accuracy of 0.873, a macro-F1 of 0.882, and a forested-wetland F1 of 0.836 on the fixed held-out test set. To interpret correlated predictors, group-aggregated SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and k-nearest-neighbor conditional replacement were used to characterize global and conditional model reliance. Among correctly classified forested-wetland samples, global reliance was greatest for temporal features and phenology, whereas conditional replacement indicated the greatest residual model reliance for hydrology, followed by topography. Direct pixel counting yielded a map-derived forested-wetland area of 686.6 km 2 , concentrated mainly in peripheral plains and hills. This framework combines process-informed feature organization with dependence-aware interpretation to support interpretable regional mapping of canopy-obscured forested wetlands.

title: ObsGate-SST: observation-gated background–detail learning for global daily sea surface temperature reconstruction
summary: Infrared cloud screening and incomplete sampling limit the process-scale use of daily satellite sea surface temperature (SST), whereas many gap-filled Level-4 analyses attenuate narrow fronts, tropical-cyclone cold wakes and short-lived warm extremes. This study presents ObsGate-SST, an observation-gated background–detail learning framework for global daily SST reconstruction. The model ingests cloud-contaminated ODYSSEA L3S SST, a valid-pixel mask and an OISST v2.1 prior. A low-frequency branch estimates the basin-scale thermal background, a high-frequency branch reconstructs gradient and texture residuals from observed pixels, and a deterministic observation gate copies all valid satellite observations exactly so that inference is restricted to missing open-ocean pixels. Training used 2000–2020 daily fields, validation used 2021–2022 and independent testing used 2023–2025. Against 2023 quality-level-5 iQuam matchups, monthly bias ranged from 0.193 to 0.291 °C, RMSE from 0.637 to 0.849 °C and correlation from 0.993 to 0.996 across 902,665 collocations. A cloud-gap-shaped withheld-observed-pixel audit isolated inferred-pixel skill: ObsGate-SST achieved the lowest pooled RMSE (0.4802 °C), while removing the low-frequency branch, high-frequency branch, gradient/detail loss and physical/prior regularization increased RMSE by 17.0 %, 9.9 %, 3.9 % and 2.0 %, respectively. Relative to DINEOF, U-Net, Swin-Unet and SegNet under common masks, ObsGate-SST better retained spectral energy, frontal continuity, marine-heatwave structure, typhoon cold wakes and equatorial Pacific gradients. These results support observation-gated multiscale learning as a physically interpretable strategy for reconstructing incomplete satellite SST without sacrificing observed-pixel fidelity.

title: Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 responses to Hansen-reported forest loss in the Peruvian Amazon: Timing and spatial sensitivity
summary: Satellite signals preceding recorded tropical forest loss are rarely tested against locations without loss. We compared the timing of Sentinel-1 co-polarised (VV) and cross-polarised (VH) backscatter and three Sentinel-2 indices (Normalized Burn Ratio, NBR; Normalized Difference Moisture Index, NDMI; Normalized Difference Red Edge index, NDRE) with Hansen Global Forest Change loss years in the Ucayali Region of the Peruvian Amazon (2019–2025). Hansen loss years served as an annual, satellite-derived reference rather than independent ground truth. Monthly time series at 819 locations with Hansen loss in 2021–2024 at the central 30 m pixel were compared with 2,588 non-loss locations using before-after analysis, superposed epoch analysis and single-change-point breakpoint detection with a pseudo-year null model. Sensitivity to spatial matching was tested with 50–250 m buffers, and canopy height from the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation was examined exploratorily. All variables declined around the Hansen loss year relative to non-loss locations, most strongly for Sentinel-2 (Cliff’s δ = − 0.66 to − 0.76; Sentinel-1: −0.27 to − 0.30). Negative breakpoints occurred at 74–82% of loss locations for the Sentinel-2 indices, mostly in the loss year. Breakpoints preceding the loss year occurred at 9.5–19.0% of loss locations, exceeding the non-loss comparison only for NBR (+4.9 percentage points) and NDRE (+3.8) at the primary penalty. Apparent pre-loss rates increased with buffer size and depended on breakpoint selection, and exploratory GEDI analysis found no detectable association between canopy height and breakpoint timing. Pre-loss satellite signals should be tested against non-loss baselines before being interpreted as early warning.

title: A multi-sensor framework for comparing and integrating optical, C-band and L-band SAR inundation products in tropical floodplain of Australia
summary: Accurate inundated landscape mapping is essential for understanding hydrological connectivity, wetland dynamics and floodplain processes in tropical environments. However, optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors often produce inconsistent inundation estimates due to differences in sensor physics, wavelength sensitivity, vegetation and cloud penetration, and analytical methods. These challenges are amplified in wet–dry tropical systems, where cloud cover, heterogeneous vegetation and seasonal flooding complicate water detection. This study develops a unified multi-sensor framework for comparing and integrating inundation products derived from Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 C-band and PALSAR-2 L-band SAR in the Daly River floodplain system in northern Australia. Inundated landscape maps were generated using supervised Random Forest classification and unsupervised multi-Otsu thresholding, followed by multi-sensor fusion analysis. Products were developed and validated using wet- and dry-season field observations and Indigenous Knowledges. Results showed strong seasonal and sensor-specific differences. Sentinel-2 provided the most balanced representation of dry-season floodplain vegetation and inundation, while Sentinel-1 achieved high wet-season overall accuracy (>0.95) under cloud-affected conditions. PALSAR-2 improved the detection of inundated vegetation and structurally complex environments, reaching an overall accuracy of 0.97. Multi-sensor evidential reasoning (fusion) improved spatial coherence and class delineation, but performance varied across sensor combinations. These findings show that optical, C-band SAR and L-band SAR inundation products are not directly interchangeable in tropical wetlands. Instead, they performed separately for each landscape. The proposed framework supports the comparison and integration of multi-sensor inundation products to enhance wetland conservation initiatives, wetland monitoring, hydrological assessment, and environmental management in data-limited tropical regions globally.

title: Neighborhood-aware retrieval of a spatial floe fragmentation index for Arctic sea ice using Sentinel-1 SAR and AMSR2
summary: Arctic sea ice fragmentation involves changes in floe area composition, spatial separation, and geometric complexity, which affect lateral melt rates and ice–ocean heat fluxes. Existing metrics primarily characterize floe size distributions or area fractions, limiting their capacity to resolve variations in the spatial arrangement of floes. We propose a spatial floe fragmentation index (SFFI) that jointly quantifies floe area composition, spatial separation, and geometric complexity. Using 416 Sentinel-1 SAR scenes spanning diverse Arctic regions and ice conditions, we extract floe contours to generate 52,074 SFFI reference labels. For samples with comparable floe area composition, higher SFFI values correspond to greater inter-floe spacing and lower circularity, demonstrating that the index captures spatial and geometric differences not represented by area composition alone. To enable daily Arctic monitoring, we develop a neighborhood-aware retrieval framework integrating AMSR2 radiometry, sea ice concentration (SIC), and neighborhood statistics, and evaluate its performance using random forest, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron models. Under the 2016–2024 SAR-scene split, XGBoost with the complete feature set achieves the best performance, with an R2 of 0.6877, an RMSE of 0.3454, and an MAE of 0.2536. Neighborhood-aware features provide relative R2 gains of 4.6% to 10.0% over the SIC-inclusive baselines. The selected model maintained robust predictive performance on the independent 2025 dataset, supporting its temporal transferability. Using the best-performing model, we generate a daily Arctic SFFI product on a 12.5 km grid for 2016–2025. Results show that SFFI captures a pronounced seasonal cycle, with high-SFFI areas expanding during the melt season and contracting during refreezing, while revealing regional differences among Arctic marginal seas.

title: Multi-temporal analysis of reflectance and vegetation index consistency between Sentinel-2 and UAS imagery over a managed broadleaved forest: implications for monitoring
summary: The comparability between satellite-based and uncrewed aerial system (UAS) imagery is critical for multiscale forest monitoring. It enables the integration of fine-resolution observations into a broader satellite-derived spatial and temporal context. Understanding this comparability supports the strategic use of centimeter-resolution UAS data to address fine-scale ecological questions, to serve as gap-filling observations within satellite-based time series during periods of absent data retrievals, and to link fine-scale canopy structural variation to landscape-level vegetation dynamics observed from space. This study investigated the spectral and vegetation index level consistency between Sentinel-2 and UAS multispectral measurements acquired over a 300 ha managed broadleaved forest in Central Europe. UAS data were collected using a fixed-wing platform equipped with a MicaSense Altum multispectral sensor and temporally matched to Sentinel-2 overpasses over a 6-month period at approximately two-week intervals. Cross-platform agreement was quantified using distribution-based similarity metrics, spatial aggregation of UAS data to Sentinel-2 spatial resolution, intrinsic correlation analysis, and single-date regression modeling. At their native spatial resolutions, UAS observations exhibited systematically higher radiometric variability and stronger distributional asymmetry than Sentinel-2 data, particularly in the red-edge band, consistent with increased sensitivity to fine-scale illumination differences and canopy structural heterogeneity, and partly reflecting radiometric differences between individual UAS flights. Spatial aggregation of UAS data reduced this variability but did not fully remove wavelength-dependent discrepancies, with the highest levels of agreement consistently observed in the green, red, and near-infrared bands. Among the vegetation indices, normalized difference metrics, particularly the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI), showed the strongest and most temporally stable cross-platform consistency across both multitemporal distributions and individual acquisition dates. In contrast, simple ratio-based indices and indices incorporating red-edge wavelengths exhibited systematic distributional shifts and reduced temporal robustness. These distributional shifts are consistent with persistent sensor-level spectral response differences rather than index-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings indicate that normalized difference indices built from spectrally well-matched bands, which largely remove radiometric differences between UAS flights, provide a robust basis for the joint exploitation of UAS and Sentinel-2 observations, enabling consistent multiscale monitoring of broadleaved forests while retaining the complementary advantages of each observational platform.

title: AHI LAI: a seamless 500 m, 4-day leaf area index dataset of the Asia-Pacific region (2015–2025) generated from geostationary Himawari-8/9 observations
summary: Vegetation plays a critical role in Earth system processes, making the monitoring of vegetation dynamics a fundamental component of global change research. Leaf area index (LAI) acts as a primary indicator for assessing vegetation canopy structure. Optical observations from polar-orbiting satellites often experience data gaps because relatively infrequent observation opportunities can coincide with regional cloud cover. High-frequency measurements from geostationary sensors, including the Himawari-8/9 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI), increase the probability of capturing valid surface signals during transient cloud-free windows. In this study, a Himawari-MODIS fusion framework integrating polar-orbiting satellite LAI observations with geostationary satellite reflectance data was developed and applied to produce a long-term, spatially seamless and high-temporal-resolution AHI-based LAI dataset for the Asia-Pacific. Biome-specific Random Forest models were trained using filtered MODIS LAI as benchmarks to estimate LAI from AHI data. A modified singular spectrum analysis (mSSA) algorithm with spatiotemporal neighbor selection was implemented to reconstruct missing values. The resulting data were subsequently downscaled utilizing spatial texture patterns derived from MODIS LAI data. This AHI LAI product features a 500 m spatial resolution and a 4-day temporal resolution, spanning from 2015 to 2025. Validation against in situ LAI measurements showed that AHI LAI achieved lower RMSE and MAE than MODIS LAI, with values of 1.781 and 1.423 compared with 2.087 and 1.647 for MODIS LAI, respectively. In cloud-prone regions and complex terrains, the AHI LAI product exhibits smoother temporal profiles and lower data dispersion compared to the MODIS LAI product. Furthermore, the AHI LAI product captures timely vegetation responses to moisture stress during drought events. The AHI LAI product may provide continuous data support for ecological monitoring and vegetation dynamics research in the Asia-Pacific region.

title: Retrieval of vegetation leaf equivalent water thickness from GF-5 hyperspectral imagery via physics-guided transfer learning
summary: Vegetation leaf equivalent water thickness (EWT) is an important indicator of plant water status and is relevant to ecological monitoring and vegetation stress assessment. However, hyperspectral retrieval of leaf EWT remains challenging because canopy structural effects and discrepancies between simulated and measured observations can limit model transferability. To address this issue, we developed a physics-guided transfer-learning framework for EWT retrieval using Gaofen-5 Advanced Hyperspectral Imager (GF-5 AHSI) data. A diverse simulation domain was constructed by coupling PROSPECT-D with the 4SAIL and 4-Scale canopy models to represent both relatively homogeneous and structurally complex vegetation. Complementary PCA-derived and physically interpretable spectral features were selected, and four base learners were integrated using out-of-fold stacking. Models were first pretrained on simulated data and subsequently fine-tuned using in-situ observations. Simulation-only pretraining achieved RMSEs of 0.083 kg/m2 on the held-out measured test set and 0.091 kg/m2 on the independent external test set. After fine-tuning, the corresponding RMSEs decreased to 0.056 and 0.071 kg/m2, respectively. Moreover, on the independent external test set, the fine-tuned ensemble reduced RMSE from 0.101 to 0.071 kg/m2 relative to measured-only modeling, further supporting improved transferability. Regional applications over Saihanba and an area within and adjacent to the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park produced spatially coherent EWT patterns, while ensemble model disagreement varied among regions and vegetation types. These results demonstrate that physics-guided simulation pretraining combined with measured-data fine-tuning provides a practical approach for improving the transferability of hyperspectral leaf-EWT retrieval under heterogeneous vegetation conditions.

title: BathyUNet++ : a bathymetry retrieval framework for high-resolution low-SNR SuperDove imagery
summary: High-spatial-resolution (HR) bathymetry is crucial for ensuring navigation safety and effective environmental management in shallow waters. However, traditional bathymetry retrieval from medium-resolution satellites yields large uncertainties under complex substrates and strong spatial heterogeneity. HR sensors, such as PlanetScope SuperDove (~3.7 m), can resolve fine-scale features but often have low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited spectral bands, leading to noisy bathymetry retrievals. To address this challenge, we developed BathyUNet++, a UNet++ architecture enhanced with spatial and channel squeeze & excitation (scSE) attention modules, for bathymetry retrieval from SuperDove imagery. While this architecture effectively leverages spatial context and complementary spectral information, it requires dense training patches. Traditional depth measurements provide sparse spatial coverage, and Airborne LiDAR Bathymetry (ALB) remains geographically limited. Therefore, we adopted a multi-source training strategy that integrates high-resolution ALB data with extensive Landsat 8/9 derived bathymetry to improve the spatial coverage and diversity of training data for SuperDove imagery. In addition, we designed a Central-Region Mean Squared Error (CMSE) that focuses on each patch's center valid receptive field to reduce instability and checkerboard artifacts often seen in satellite products generated via patch-based processing. Independent validation shows that BathyUNet++ achieves high-accuracy bathymetry retrievals, with median absolute percentage differences below 15% compared with independent depth measurements from ICESat-2 and ALB. Notably, BathyUNet++ substantially reduces noise compared with bathymetry maps derived from pixel-based algorithms, yielding spatially consistent bathymetry maps. The proposed framework overcomes the limitations of low-SNR data and can be readily adapted to other HR sensors, offering a promising solution for the broader application of HR bathymetry retrieval in optically shallow waters.

title: Integrating vegetation phenology and SWOT-derived surface water dynamics for improved county-scale winter wheat yield prediction
summary: Winter wheat yield is shaped by crop growth status and surface hydrological conditions. However, remote-sensing approaches based primarily on vegetation index (VI) time series may not fully represent the surrounding surface-water environment in county-scale yield prediction. We integrated growth-stage VI features with surface-water dynamics derived from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission to predict county-level winter wheat yield in Henan Province, China. We evaluated direct feature fusion, same-year residual correction, and target-year residual correction following cross-year VI extrapolation using outer ten-fold cross-validation. Inner five-fold cross-fitting generated same-year VI residual targets exclusively within each outer training set. The VI-only model achieved R2 = 0.772, RMSE = 0.688 t ha−1, and MAE = 0.510 t ha−1. Direct incorporation of SWOT features reduced predictive accuracy, with R2 = 0.749, RMSE = 0.721 t ha−1, and MAE = 0.547 t ha−1. By contrast, SWOT-based residual correction yielded a clearer improvement in same-year prediction, increasing R2 to 0.795 and reducing RMSE to 0.652 t ha−1. The historical VI model was trained on 2010–2021, independently tested on 2022–2023, and extrapolated to 2024, where it achieved R2 = 0.676, RMSE = 0.819 t ha−1, and MAE = 0.611 t ha−1. Calibrated using observed 2024 yields from training counties and evaluated on held-out 2024 counties, subsequent target-year residual correction with concurrent SWOT features increased R2 to 0.749 and reduced RMSE and MAE to 0.722 and 0.524 t ha−1, respectively. SHAP analysis showed that SWOT contributions were concentrated during seeding, emergence, overwintering, green, heading–flowering, and filling and varied by spatial scale and prediction scenario. Overall, SWOT-derived surface-water observations provided complementary predictive information relative to the evaluated VI baselines, particularly for target-year spatial calibration. Their broader applicability across regions, crops, and years remains to be established through independent validation.

title: Coarse-to-fine physics-guided reconstruction of gridded sea level anomalies from HY-2B/C/D altimetry
summary: The capability of the Chinese HY-2B/C/D altimeter constellation for gridded sea level anomaly (SLA) reconstruction using only HY-2 observations remains insufficiently evaluated. This study presents a physics-guided framework designed for near-real-time (NRT) SLA reconstruction in the Northwest Pacific and retrospectively evaluates it using 2022−2025 HY-2B/C/D observations. The framework combines an OI-derived coarse background with deep-learning refinement, with target-period reconstruction driven solely by HY-2B/C/D along-track data. Validation against an identical set of 1255 independent tide-gauge observations yields mean RMSE of 0.051 m and a mean correlation coefficient (r) of 0.83 over 12 tide-gauge stations. Inter-product comparisons during 2022−2025 show closer agreement with the DUACS DT and NRT products than with NSOAS, although differences in SLA reference conventions and geophysical correction standards among the products should be considered when interpreting regional discrepancies. Scale-dependent evaluation using SARAL/AltiKa along-track observations indicates a mean effective spatial resolution of approximately 300 km. Dynamical consistency is further assessed against surface-drifter observations using geostrophic velocity anomaly magnitude, yielding mean RMSE of 0.181 m s−1 and r of 0.54. These results demonstrate that spatially coherent and dynamically plausible daily SLA fields can be reconstructed with HY-2B/C/D as the sole altimetric observations during the target period, supporting the potential of the proposed framework for NRT SLA reconstruction under sparse observational constraints.

title: Gravity-conditioned diffusion for seafloor bathymetric resolution enhancement
summary: Global bathymetric products such as SRTM15+ provide extensive ocean coverage but cannot resolve many fine-scale seafloor features captured by shipborne multibeam surveys. Generative reconstruction methods can reconstruct more detailed terrain, but they may also introduce plausible-looking structures that are not supported by observations. We propose GravBathy-Diff, a conditional diffusion framework that uses observed low-resolution bathymetry as its primary input and incorporates satellite-altimetry-derived marine gravity as an auxiliary physical constraint. The gravity-differential enhancement module jointly encodes bathymetry, terrain derivatives, and the co-registered gravity field at the input stage. Gravity-conditioned time–frequency modulation regulates the contribution of gravity across diffusion stages and feature bands, while gravity-guided attention focuses this information on the spatial locations and feature channels where it is most useful. Deflections of the vertical, gravity anomalies, and vertical gravity gradients derived from Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) wide-swath altimetry are compared as alternative conditioning fields. Experiments are conducted on real SRTM15+ –multibeam bathymetry pairs from four ocean regions and assessed using depth error, perceptual similarity, terrain derivatives, and spectral fidelity. GravBathy-Diff achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated regression, adversarial, and diffusion methods, with the exception of one regional gradient-RMSE result. It ranks first on all six metrics averaged over four additional ocean areas and remains effective on an independent public digital elevation model (DEM) benchmark at 4×. Among the three gravity representations, the vertical gravity gradient provides the most effective guidance for reconstructing local relief. These results show that marine gravity can support the recovery of fine-scale seafloor structure while reducing high-frequency artifacts that are inconsistent with the available observations.
